body.input: Well, I'll tell you that I think, well, let me just say that, that, that what you would predict

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: about, for example, the performance of the two of them in the debates, and I wrote an op-ed for

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: the New York Times actually before the second debate. And it played out really pretty much as

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: I thought that it would based on research. It's not like I'm like a great fortune teller or

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: anything. It's just, I was just applying the research, which was that when a woman

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: a woman's people make internal attributions, it's called, they, they infer that the facial movements

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: and body posture and vocalizations of a woman reflect her interstate. But for a man, they're

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: more likely to assume that they reflect his response to the situation. It doesn't say anything

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: about him. It says something about the situation he's in. That's brilliant. Now for the thing

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: that you are, that you were describing about Hillary Clinton, I think a lot of people think

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: Clinton, I think a lot of people experienced, but it's also in line with research, which shows,

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: and particularly research actually on, about teaching evaluations is one place that you really

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: see it, where the expectation is that a woman will be nurturant and that a man, there's just

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: no expectation for him to be nurturant. So he's, you know, if he is nurturant, he gets points.

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: If he's not, he gets points. They're just different points, right? Whereas for a woman,

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: especially a woman who's an authority figure, she's really in a catch-22. Because if she's

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: serious, she's a bitch. And if she's empathic, then she's weak. Right. That's brilliant. I mean,

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: one of the bigger questions to ask here. So that's one example where our construction of concepts

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: gets us in trouble. Right. But remember I said science and philosophy are like tools for living.

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: So I learned recently that if you ask me, what is my intuition about what regulates my eating,

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: I will say carbohydrates. I love carbohydrates. I love pasta. I love bread. I just love carbohydrates.

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: Yeah. But actually research shows, and it's beautiful research. I love this research

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: because it so violates my own like deeply, deeply held beliefs about myself, that most animals on

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: this planet who have been studied, and there are many, actually eat to regulate their protein

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: intake. So you will overeat carbohydrates in order to get enough protein. And this research has been

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: done with humans, very beautiful research, with humans, with crickets, with like bonobos. I mean,

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: just like all these different animals, not bonobos, but I think like baboons. Now, I have no

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: intuition about that. And even now as I regulate my eating, I just have no intuition. I can't feel it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: What I feel is only about the carbohydrates. It feels like you're regulating around carbohydrates,

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: not the protein. Yeah. But in fact, actually what I am doing, if I am like most animals on the planet,

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: I am regulating around protein. So knowing this, what do I do? I correct my behavior to actually

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: deliberately try to focus on the protein. This is the idea behind bias training, right? Like if you...

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: I also did not experience Hillary Clinton as the warmest candidate. However, you can use consistent

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: science, consistent scientific findings to organize your behavior. That doesn't mean that

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: rationality is the absence of emotion, because sometimes emotion or any feelings in general,

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: not the same thing as emotion, that's another topic, but are a source of information and their

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: wisdom and helpful. So I'm not saying that... But what I am saying is that if you have a deeply held

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: belief and the evidence shows that you're wrong, then you're wrong. It doesn't really matter how

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: confident you feel. That confidence could be also explained by science, right? So it would be the

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: same thing as if I... Regardless of whether someone is a Republican, like Charlie Baker, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: Regardless of whether somebody is a Republican or a Democrat, if that person has a record that you

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: can see is consistent with what you believe, then that is information that you can act on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: Yeah. And then try to... I mean, this is kind of what empathy is in open-mindedness, is try to

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: consider that the set of concepts that your brain has constructed through which you are now

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: perceiving the world is not painting the full picture. I mean, this is now true for basically...

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: It doesn't have to be men and women. It could be basically the prism through which we perceive

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: actually the political discourse, right? Absolutely. So here's the thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: Absolutely. So here's what I would say. There are scientists who will talk to you about cognitive

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: empathy and emotional empathy and I prefer to think of it... I think the evidence is more

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: consistent with what I'm about to say, which is that your brain is always making predictions

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: using your own past experience and what you've learned from books and movies and other people

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: telling you about their experiences and so on. And if your brain cannot make a concept

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: to make sense of those, anticipate what those sense data are and make sense of them,

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: you will be experientially blind. So when I'm giving lectures to people, I'll show them like

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: a blobby black and white image and they're experientially blind to the image. They can't

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: see anything in it. And then I show them a photograph and then I show them the image again,

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: the blobby image, and then they see actually an object in it. But the image is the same.

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: They're actually adding, their predictions now are adding, right? Or anybody who's...

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: Anybody who's learned a language, a second language after their first language also has

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: this experience of things that initially sound like sounds that they can't quite make sense of,

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: eventually come to make... They eventually come to make sense of them. And in fact,

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: there are really cool examples of people who were like born blind because they have cataracts or

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: they have corneal damage so that no light is reaching the brain. And then they have an

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: operation and then light reaches the brain and they can't see. For days and weeks and sometimes

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: years, they are experientially blind to certain things. So what happens with empathy, right? Is

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: that your brain is making a prediction. And if it doesn't have the capacity to make... If you don't

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: share... If you're not similar, remember, you mean, categories are instances which are similar in

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: some way. If you are not similar enough to that person, you will have a hard time making a

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: prediction about what they feel. You will be experientially blind to what they feel.

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: In the United States, children of color are under prescribed medicine by their physicians.

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: This has been documented. It's not that the physicians are racist necessarily,

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: but they might be experientially blind.

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: The same thing is true of male physicians with female patients. I could tell you some

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: hair-raising stories really that where people die as a consequence of a physician making the wrong

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: inference, the wrong prediction because of being experientially blind.

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: So empathy is not magic. We make inferences about each other, about what each other's feeling and

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: thinking in this culture more than... There are some cultures where people have what's called

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: opacity of mind, where they will make a prediction about someone else's actions, but they're not

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: inferring anything about the internal state of the person. They're just making a prediction

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: about the internal state of that person. But in our culture, we're constantly making inferences.

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: What is this person thinking? And we're not doing it necessarily consciously,

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: but we're just doing it really automatically using our predictions, what we know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: If you expose yourself to information which is very different from somebody else,

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: I mean, really what we have is we have different cultures in this country right now that are...

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: There are a number of reasons for this. I mean, part of it is, I don't know if you saw the social

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: dilemma, the Netflix... Heard about it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: Yeah, it's a great... It's really great documentary and...

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: About what social networks are doing to our society.

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: Yeah, yeah. But nothing... No phenomenon has a simple single cause. There are multiple

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: small causes which all add up to a perfect storm. That's just how most things work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: And so the fact that machine learning algorithms are serving people up information on social media

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: that is consistent with what they've already viewed and making... Is part of the reason that

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: you have these silos, but it's not the only reason why you have these silos, I think. There are other

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: things afoot that enhance people's inability to even have a decent conversation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: Yeah. I mean, okay, so many things you said are just brilliant. So the experiment, experiential

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: blindness, but also from my perspective, I preach and I try to practice empathy a lot.

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: And something about the way you've explained it makes me almost see as a kind of exercise that

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: we should all do, like to train, like to add experiences to the brain to expand this capacity

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: to predict more effectively. Absolutely. So what I do is kind of like a method acting thing, which is

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: I imagine what the life of a person is like. Just think. I mean, this is something you see with

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: Black Lives Matter and police officers. It feels like they're both... Not both, but because of

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: martial arts and so on, I have a lot of friends who are cops. They don't necessarily have empathy

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: or visualize the experience of the other. Certainly, currently, unfortunately, people aren't doing that

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: with police officers. They're not imagining, they're not empathizing or putting themselves

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: in the shoes of a police officer to realize how difficult that job is, how dangerous it is,

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: how difficult it is to maintain calm and under so much uncertainty, all those kinds of things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: But there's more, there's even... That's all that's true, but I think that there's even more,

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: there's even more to be said there. I mean, from a predicting brain standpoint, there's even more

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: that can be said there. So I don't know if you want to go down that path or you want to stick

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: on empathy, but I will also say that one of the things that I was most gratified by, I still am

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: receiving... It's been more than three and a half years since How Motions Are Made came out, and I'm

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: still receiving daily emails from people. So that's gratifying. But one of the most gratifying

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: emails I received was from a police officer in Texas who told me that he thought that

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: How Motions Are Made contained information that would be really helpful to resolving

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: some of these difficulties. And he hadn't even read my op-ed piece about when is a gun not a gun,

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: and using what we know about the science of perception from a prediction standpoint,

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: like the brain is a predictor, to understand a little differently what might be happening

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: in these circumstances. So it's hard to talk about because

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: everyone gets mad at you when you talk about this. And there is a way to understand this,

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: which has profound empathy for the suffering of people of color, and that definitely is in

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: line with Black Lives Matter at the same time as understanding the really difficult situation

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: that police officers find themselves in. And I'm not talking about this bad apple or that bad

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: apple. I'm not talking about police officers who are necessarily shooting people in the back as

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: they run away. I'm talking about the cases of really good, well-meaning cops who have the kind

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: of predicting brain that everybody else has. They're in a really difficult situation that I

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: think both they and the people who are harmed don't realize. The way that these situations

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: are constructed, I think it's just, there's a lot to be said there, I guess, is what I want to say.

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: Is there something we can try to say in a sense, like from the perspective of the predictive brain,

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: which is a fascinating perspective to take on this, all the protests that are going on,

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: there seems to be a concept of a police officer being built.

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: No, I think that concept is there. But it's gaining strength. So it's being re-

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: I mean, it is there. Yeah, for sure. Yeah, for sure. I think that that's right. I think that

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: there's a shift in the stereotype of what I would say is a stereotype. There's a stereotype of

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: a black man in this country that's always in movies and television, not always, but largely,

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: that many people watch. I mean, you think you're watching a 10 o'clock drama and all you're doing

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: is kicking back and relaxing, but actually you're having certain predictions reinforced

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: and others not. And what's happening now with police is the same thing, that there are certain

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: stereotypes of a police officer that are being abandoned and other stereotypes that are being

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: reinforced by what you see happening. All I'll say is that if you remember, I mean,

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: there's a lot to say about this really, that regardless of whether it makes people mad or

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: not, I mean, the science is what it is. Just remember what I said, the brain makes predictions

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: about internal changes in the body first and then it starts to prepare motor action.

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: And then it makes a prediction about what you will see and hear and feel based on those actions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: Okay? So it's also the case that we didn't talk about is that sensory sampling, like your brain's

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: ability to sample what's out there is yoked to your heart rate. It's yoked to your heartbeats.

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: There are certain phases of the heartbeat where it's easier for you to see what's happening in

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: the world than in others. And so if your heart rate goes through the roof,

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: you will be more likely to just go with your prediction and not correct based on what's out

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: there because you're actually literally not seeing as well. Or you will see things that

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: aren't there basically. Is there something that we could say in by way of advice for

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: when this episode is released in the chaos of emotion? Sorry, I don't know about a term

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: that's just flying around on social media. Well, I actually think it is emotion in the following

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: sense. It sounds a little bit artificial in the way that I'm about to say it, but I really think

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: that this is what's happening. One thing we haven't talked about is brains evolved,

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: didn't evolve for you to see, they didn't evolve for you to hear, they didn't evolve for you to

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: feel, they evolved to control your body. That's why you have a brain. You have a brain so they

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: can control your body. And the metaphor, the scientific term for predictively controlling

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: your body is allostasis. Your brain is attempting to anticipate the needs of your body and meet

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: those needs before they arise so that you can act as you need to act. And the metaphor that I use

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: is a body budget. Your brain is running a budget for your body. It's not budgeting money, it's

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: budgeting glucose and salt and water. And instead of having one or two bank accounts, it has

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: gazillions. There are all these systems in your body that have to be kept in balance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: And it's monitoring very closely, it's making predictions about when is it good to spend and

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: when is it good to save and what would be a good investment and am I going to get a return on my

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: investment? Whenever people talk about reward or reward prediction error or anything to do with

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: reward or punishment, they're talking about the body budget. They're talking about your brain's

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: predictions about whether or not there will be a deposit or withdrawal. So when your brain is running

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: a deficit in your body budgets, you have some kind of metabolic imbalance, you experience that as

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: discomfort. You experience that as distress. When things are chaotic, you can't predict what's

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: going to happen next. So I have this absolutely brilliant scientist working in my lab. His name

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: is Jordan Terrio and he's published this really terrific paper on a sense of should. Why do we

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: have social rules? Why do we adhere to social norms? It's because if I make myself predictable

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: to you, then you are predictable to me. And if you're predictable to me, that's good because

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: that is less metabolically expensive for me. Novelty or unpredictability at the extreme

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: is expensive. And if it goes on for long enough, what happens is first of all, you will feel really

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

body.input: jittery and antsy, which we describe as anxiety. It isn't necessarily anxiety. It could be just

metadata.title: Podcast: Lisa Feldman Barrett: Counterintuitive Ideas About How the Brain Works | Lex Fridman Podcast #129

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And now here's my conversation with Richard Karp.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: You wrote that at the age of 13,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: you were first exposed to plain geometry

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and was wonderstruck by the power and elegance

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: of form of proofs.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Are there problems, proofs, properties, ideas

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: in plain geometry that from that time

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: that you remember being mesmerized by

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: or just enjoying to go through to prove various aspects?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So Michael Rabin told me this story about an experience

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: he had when he was a young student

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: who was tossed out of his classroom for bad behavior

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and was wandering through the corridors of his school

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and came upon two older students

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: who were studying the problem of finding

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: the shortest distance between two non-overlapping circles.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And Michael thought about it and said,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: you take the straight line between the two centers

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and the segment between the two circles is the shortest

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: because a straight line is the shortest distance

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: between the two centers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And any other line connecting the circles

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: would be on a longer line.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And I thought, and he thought, and I agreed

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: that this was just elegance,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: the pure reasoning could come up with such a result.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Certainly the shortest distance

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: from the two centers of the circles is a straight line.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Could you once again say,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: what's the next step in that proof?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Well, any segment joining the two circles,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: if you extend it by taking the radius on each side,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: you get a segment with a path with three edges

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: which connects the two centers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And this has to be at least as long as the shortest path,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: which is the straight line.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: The straight line, yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Wow, yeah, that's quite simple.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So what is it about that elegance

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: that you just find compelling?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Well, just that you could establish a fact

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: about geometry beyond dispute by pure reasoning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: I also enjoy the challenge of solving puzzles

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: in plain geometry.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: It was much more fun than the earlier mathematics courses

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: which were mostly about arithmetic operations

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and manipulating them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Was there something about geometry itself,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: the slightly visual component of it

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: that you can visualize?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Oh, yes, absolutely.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Although I lacked three-dimensional vision.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: I wasn't very good at three-dimensional vision.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: You mean being able to visualize three-dimensional objects?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Three-dimensional objects or surfaces, hyperplanes

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So there I didn't have an intuition,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: but for example, the fact that the sum of the angles

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: of a triangle is 180 degrees is proved convincingly

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and it comes as a surprise that that can be done.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Why is that surprising?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Well, it is a surprising idea, I suppose.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Why is that proved difficult?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: It's not.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: That's the point.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: It's so easy and yet it's so convincing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Do you remember what is the proof

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: that it adds up to 180?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: You start at a corner and draw a line parallel

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: to the opposite side and that line sort of trisects

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: the angle between the other two sides.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And you get a half plane which has to add up to 180 degrees.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And it consists in the angles by the equality

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: of alternate angles, what's it called?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: You get a correspondence between the angles created

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: by the side along the side of the triangle

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and the three angles of the triangle.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Has geometry had an impact on, when you look into

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: the future of your work with combinatorial algorithms,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: has it had some kind of impact in terms of, yeah,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: being able, the puzzles, the visual aspects

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: that were first so compelling to you?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Not Euclidean geometry particularly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: I think I use tools like linear programming

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and integer programming a lot.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And but those require high dimensional visualization.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And so I tend to go by the algebraic properties.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Right, you go by the linear algebra

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and not by the visualization.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Well, the interpretation in terms of, for example,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: finding the highest point on a polyhedron

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: as in linear programming is motivating.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But again, I don't have the high dimensional intuition

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: that would particularly inform me.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So I sort of lean on the algebra.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So to linger on that point, what kind of visualization

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: do you do when you're trying to think about,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: well, get to combinatorial algorithms,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: but just algorithms in general?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: What's inside your mind when you're thinking

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: about designing algorithms?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Or even just tackling any mathematical problem?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Well, I think that usually an algorithm

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: involves a repetition of some inner loop.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And so I can sort of visualize the distance

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: from the desired solution as iteratively reducing

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: until you finally hit the exact solution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And try to take steps that get you closer to the-

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Try to take steps that get closer

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and having the certainty of converging.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So it's basically the mechanics of the algorithm

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: is often very simple.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But especially when you're trying something out

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: on the computer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So for example, I did some work

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: on the traveling salesman problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And I could see there was a particular function

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: that had to be minimized.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And it was fascinating to see the successive approaches

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: to the optimum.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: You mean, so first of all, traveling salesman problem

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: is where you have to visit every city

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: without ever, the only ones.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yeah, that's right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Find the shortest path through a set of cities.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yeah, which is sort of a canonical standard,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: a really nice problem that's really hard.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Right, exactly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So can you say again, what was nice about the objective,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: being able to think about the objective function there

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and maximizing it or minimizing it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Well, just that as the algorithm proceeded,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: you were making progress, continual progress.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And eventually getting to the optimum point.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So there's two parts, maybe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Maybe you can correct me.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But first is like getting an intuition

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: about what the solution would look like.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And, or even maybe coming up with a solution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And two is proving that this thing

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: is actually going to be pretty good.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: What part is harder for you?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Where's the magic happen?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Is it in the first sets of intuitions?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Or is it in the messy details of actually showing

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: that it is going to get to the exact solution

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and it's gonna run at a certain complexity?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Well, the magic is just the fact that the gap

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: from the optimum decreases monotonically

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and you can see it happening.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And various metrics of what's going on

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: are improving all along until finally you hit the optimum.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Perhaps later we'll talk about the assignment problem

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and I can illustrate.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: It illustrates a little better.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Now zooming out again, as you write,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Don Knuth has called attention to a breed of people

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: who derive great aesthetic pleasure

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: from contemplating the structure

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: of computational processes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So Don calls these folks geeks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And you write that you remember the moment

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: you realized you were such a person,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: you were shown the Hungarian algorithm

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: to solve the assignment problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So perhaps you can explain what the assignment problem is

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and what the Hungarian algorithm is.

body.input: So in the assignment problem,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So what you do is to depend on the observation
