body.input: That would be what's called a complete graph.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: No, I mean within that clique.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Within that clique, yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: They're all friends.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So a complete graph is when?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Everybody's friendly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: As everybody is friends with everybody.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So the problem might be to determine

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: whether in a given graph there exists a clique

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: of a certain size.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Well that turns out to be a very hard problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But if somebody hands you a clique

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and asks you to check whether it is,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: hands you a set of vertices and asks you to check

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: whether it's a clique, you could do that simply

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: by exhaustively looking at all of the edges

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: between the vertices and the clique

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and verifying that they're all there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And that's a polynomial time algorithm.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And that's a polynomial, so the problem of finding

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: the clique appears to be extremely hard,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: but the problem of verifying a clique to see

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: if it reaches a target number of vertices

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: is easy to verify.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So finding the clique is hard, checking it is easy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Problems of that nature are called the

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: non-deterministic polynomial time algorithms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And that's the class NP.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And what about NP complete and NP hard?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Okay, let's talk about problems where you're getting

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: a yes or no answer rather than a numerical value.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So either there is a perfect matching

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: of the boys with the girls or there isn't.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: It's clear that every problem in P is also in NP.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: If you can solve the problem exactly,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: then you can certainly verify the solution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: On the other hand, there are problems in the class NP.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: This is the class of problems that are easy to check,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: although they may be hard to solve.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: It's not at all clear that problems in NP lie in P.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So for example, if we're looking at scheduling classes

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: at a school, the fact that you can verify

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: when handed a schedule for the school

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: whether it meets all the requirements,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: that doesn't mean that you can find the schedule rapidly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So intuitively, NP, non-deterministic polynomial,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: checking rather than finding, is going to be harder than,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: is going to include, is easier, checking is easier,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and therefore the class of problems that can be checked

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: appears to be much larger than the class of problems

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: that can be solved.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And then you keep adding appears to and sort of these

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: additional words that designate that we don't know for sure yet.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: We don't know for sure.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So the theoretical question, which is considered

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: to be the most central problem in theoretical computer science

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: or at least computational complexity theory,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: combinatorial algorithm theory,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: the question is whether P is equal to NP.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: If P were equal to NP, it would be amazing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: It would mean that every problem where a solution

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: can be rapidly checked can actually be solved

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: in polynomial time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: We don't really believe that's true.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: If you're scheduling classes at a school,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: we expect that if somebody hands you a satisfying schedule,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: you can verify that it works.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: That doesn't mean that you should be able to find such a schedule.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So intuitively, NP encompasses a lot more problems than P.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So can we take a small tangent and break apart that intuition?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So do you first of all think that the biggest sort of open problem

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: in computer science, maybe mathematics, is whether P equals NP?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Do you think P equals NP or do you think P is not equal to NP?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: If you had to bet all your money on it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: I would bet that P is unequal to NP simply because there are problems

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: that have been around for centuries and have been studied intensively

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: in mathematics and even more so in the last 50 years

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: since the P versus NP was stated.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And no polynomial time algorithms have been found

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: for these easy to check problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So one example is a problem that goes back to the mathematician Gauss

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: who was interested in factoring large numbers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So we know what a number is prime if it cannot be written as the product

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: of two or more numbers unequal to one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So if we can factor a number like 91, it's 7 times 13.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But if I give you 20-digit or 30-digit numbers, you're probably going to be

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: at a loss to have any idea whether they can be factored.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So the problem of factoring very large numbers does not appear

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: to have an efficient solution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But once you have found the factors, express the number as a product

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: of two smaller numbers, you can quickly verify that they are factors of the number.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And your intuition is a lot of people finding, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: a lot of brilliant people have tried to find algorithms for this one particular problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: There's many others like it that are really well studied

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and it would be great to find an efficient algorithm for.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Right. And in fact, we have some results that I was instrumental in obtaining

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: following up on work by the mathematician Stephen Cook

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: to show that within the class NP of easy to check problems,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: there's a huge number that are equivalent in the sense that either all of them

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: or none of them lie in P. And this happens only if P is equal to NP.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So if P is unequal to NP, we would also know that virtually all the standard

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: combinatorial problems, if P is unequal to NP, none of them can be solved in polynomial time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Can you explain how that's possible to tie together so many problems

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: in a nice bunch that if one is proven to be efficient, then all are?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: The first and most important stage of progress was a result by Stephen Cook,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: who showed that a certain problem called the satisfiability problem of propositional logic

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: is as hard as any problem in the class P.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So the propositional logic problem is expressed in terms of expressions

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: involving the logical operations and or and not operating on variables

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: that can be either true or false. So an instance of the problem would be

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: some formula involving and or and not. And the question would be whether there is

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: an assignment of truth values to the variables in the problem that would make the formula true.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So for example, if I take the formula a or b and a or not b and not a or b and not a or not b

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and take the conjunction of all four of those so-called expressions, you can determine

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: that no assignment of truth values to the variables a and b will allow that conjunction

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: of what are called clauses to be true. So that's an example of a formula in

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: propositional logic involving expressions based on the operations and or and not.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: That's an example of a problem which is not satisfiable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: There is no solution that satisfies all of those constraints.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And that's like one of the cleanest and fundamental problems in computer science.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: It's like a nice statement of a really hard problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: It's a nice statement of a really hard problem. And what Cook showed is that

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: every problem in NP can be re-expressed as an instance of the satisfiability problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So to do that, he used the observation that a very simple abstract machine

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: called the Turing machine can be used to describe any algorithm.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: An algorithm for any realistic computer can be translated into an equivalent algorithm

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: on one of these Turing machines which are extremely simple.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So a Turing machine, there's a tape and you can walk along that tape.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yeah, you have data on a tape and you have basic instructions, a finite list of instructions

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: which say if you're reading a particular symbol on the tape and you're in a particular state,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: then you can move to a different state and change the state of the element that you were looking at,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: the cell of the tape that you were looking at.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And that was like a metaphor and a mathematical construct that Turing put together

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: to represent all possible computation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: All possible computation. Now one of these so-called Turing machines is too simple to be useful in practice.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But for theoretical purposes, we can depend on the fact that an algorithm for any computer

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: can be translated into one that would run on a Turing machine.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And then using that fact, he could sort of describe any possible non-deterministic polynomial time algorithm,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: any algorithm for a problem in P could be expressed as a sequence of moves of the Turing machine

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: described in terms of reading a symbol on the tape while you're in a given state

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and moving to a new state and leaving behind a new symbol.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And given that fact that any non-deterministic polynomial time algorithm can be described by a list of such instructions,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: you could translate the problem into the language of the satisfiability problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Is that amazing to you, by the way, if you take yourself back when you were first thinking about this space of problems?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: How amazing is that?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: It's astonishing when you look at Cook's proof, it's not too difficult to sort of figure out why this is so.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But the implications are staggering.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: It tells us that this, of all the problems in P, all the problems where solutions are easy to check,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: they can all be rewritten in terms of the satisfiability problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yes, in adding so much more weight to the P equals NP question, because all it takes is to show that one algorithm in this class.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So the P versus NP can be re-expressed as simply asking whether the satisfiability problem of propositional logic is solvable in polynomial time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But there's more.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: I encountered Cook's paper when he published it in a conference in 1971.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yeah, so when I saw Cook's paper and saw this reduction of each of the problems in NP by a uniform method to the satisfiability problem of propositional logic,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: that meant that the satisfiability problem was a universal combinatorial problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And it occurred to me through experience I had had in trying to solve other combinatorial problems,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: that there were many other problems which seemed to have that universal structure.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And so I began looking for reductions from the satisfiability to other problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: One of the other problems would be the so-called integer programming problem of determining whether there's a solution to a set of linear inequalities involving integer variables.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So it's like linear programming, but there's a constraint that the variables must remain integers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Integers, in fact, must be the 0 or 1, could only take on those values.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And that makes the problem much harder.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yes, that makes the problem much harder.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And it was not difficult to show that the satisfiability problem can be restated as an integer programming problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So can you pause on that? Was that one of the first mappings that you tried to do?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And how hard is that mapping? You said it wasn't hard to show, but that's a big leap.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: It is a big leap, yeah. Well, let me give you another example.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Another problem in NP is whether a graph contains a clique of a given size.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And now the question is, can we reduce the propositional logic problem to the problem of whether there's a clique of a certain size?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Well, if you look at the propositional logic problem, it can be expressed as a number of clauses, each of which is of the form A or B or C,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: where A is either one of the variables in the problem or the negation of one of the variables.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And an instance of the propositional logic problem can be rewritten using operations of Boolean logic,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: can be rewritten as the conjunction of a set of clauses, the and of a set of ors,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: where each clause is a disjunction, an or of variables or negated variables.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So the question in the satisfiability problem is whether those clauses can be simultaneously satisfied.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Now, to satisfy all those clauses, you have to find one of the terms in each clause,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: which is going to be true in your truth assignment, but you can't make the same variable both true and false.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So if you have the variable A in one clause and you want to satisfy that clause by making A true,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: you can't also make the complement of A true in some other clause.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And so the goal is to make every single clause true if it's possible to satisfy this, and the way you make it true is at least...

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: One term in the clause must be true.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Got it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So now we... to convert this problem to something called the independent set problem, where you're just sort of asking for a set of vertices in a graph,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: such that no two of them are adjacent, sort of the opposite of the clique problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So we've seen that we can now express that as finding a set of terms, one in each clause,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: without picking both the variable and the negation of that variable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Because if the variable is assigned the truth value, the negated variable has to have the opposite truth value.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And so we can construct a graph where the vertices are the terms in all of the clauses,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and you have an edge between two terms, an edge between two occurrences of terms,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: either if they're both in the same clause, because you're only picking one element from each clause,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and also an edge between them if they represent opposite values of the same variable,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: because you can't make a variable both true and false.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And so you get a graph where you have all of these occurrences of variables, you have edges,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: which mean that you're not allowed to choose both ends of the edge, either because they're in the same clause, or they're negations of one another.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Right. And that's a really powerful idea that you can take a graph and connect it to a logic equation somehow,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and do that mapping for all possible formulations of a particular problem on a graph.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: I mean, that still is hard for me to believe that that's possible.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Like, what do you make of that, that there's such a union of, there's such a friendship among all these problems across,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: that somehow are akin to combinatorial algorithms, that they're all somehow related?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: I know it can be proven, but what do you make of it, that that's true?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Well, that they just have the same expressive power. You can take any one of them and translate it into the terms of the other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: The fact that they have the same expressive power also somehow means that they can be translatable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Right. And what I did in the 1971 paper was to take 21 fundamental problems, commonly occurring problems of packing, covering, matching, and so forth,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: or lying in the class NP and show that the satisfiability problem can be re-expressed as any of those, that any of those have the same expressive power.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And that was like throwing down the gauntlet or saying, there's probably many more problems like this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But that's just saying that, look, that they're all the same.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But not exactly. They're all the same in terms of whether they are rich enough to express any of the others.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But that doesn't mean that they have the same computational complexity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But what we can say is that either all of these problems or none of them are solvable in polynomial time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yeah. So where does NP completeness and NP hard in this class?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Oh, that's just a small technicality.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So when we're talking about decision problems, that means that the answer is just yes or no.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: There was a clique of size 15 or there's not a clique of size 15.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: On the other hand, an optimization problem would be asking, find the largest clique.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: The answer would not be yes or no. It would be 15.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So when you're putting a valuation on the different solutions and you're asking for the one with the highest valuation,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: that's an optimization problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And there's a very close affinity between the two kinds of problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But the counterpart of being the hardest decision problem, the hardest yes-no problem,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: the counterpart of that is to minimize or maximize an objective function.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And so a problem that's hardest in the class when viewed in terms of optimization, those are called NP hard rather than NP complete.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And NP complete is for decision problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And NP complete is for decision problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So if somebody shows that P equals NP, what do you think that proof will look like if you were to put on yourself,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: if it's possible to show that as a proof or to demonstrate an algorithm?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: All I can say is that it will involve concepts that we do not now have and approaches that we don't have.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Do you think those concepts are out there in terms of inside complexity theory, inside of computational analysis of algorithms?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Do you think there's concepts that are totally outside of the box that we haven't considered yet?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: I think that if there is a proof that P is equal to NP or that P is not equal to NP, it will depend on concepts that are now outside the box.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Now, if that's shown either way, P equals NP or P not, well, actually P equals NP, what impact?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: You kind of mentioned a little bit, but can you can you linger on it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: What kind of impact would it have on theoretical computer science and perhaps software systems in general?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Well, I think it would have enormous impact on the on the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And in either way case, if P is unequal to NP, which is what we expect,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: then we know that we're in that for the great majority of the combinatorial problems that come up,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: since they're known to be NP complete, we're not going to be able to solve them by efficient algorithms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: However, there's a little bit of hope in that it may be that we can solve most instances.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: All we know is that if a problem is not in P, then it can't be solved efficiently on all instances.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But basically it will if we find that P is unequal to NP,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: it will mean that we can't expect always to get the optimal solutions to these problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And we have to depend on heuristics that perhaps work most of the time or give us good approximate solutions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So we would turn our eye towards the heuristics with a little bit more acceptance and comfort on our hearts.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Exactly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: OK, so let me ask a romanticized question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: What to you is one of the most or the most beautiful combinatorial algorithm in your own life

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: or just in general in the field that you've ever come across or have developed yourself?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: I like the stable matching problem, the stable marriage problem very much.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: What's the stable matching problem?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Imagine that you want to marry off N boys with N girls.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And each boy has an ordered list of his preferences among the girls, his first choice, his second choice, through her Nth choice.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And each girl also has an ordering of the boys, his first choice, second choice, and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And we'll say that a one-to-one matching of the boys with the girls is stable if there are no two couples in the matching,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: such that the boy in the first couple prefers the girl in the second couple to her mate, and she prefers the boy to her current mate.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: In other words, the matching is stable if there is no pair who want to run away with each other, leaving their partners behind.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Gosh, yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Actually, this is relevant to matching residents with hospitals and some other real-life problems,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: although not quite in the form that I described.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So it turns out that for any set of preferences, a stable matching exists.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And moreover, it can be computed by a simple algorithm in which each boy starts making proposals to girls.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And if a girl receives a proposal, she accepts it tentatively, but she can drop it later if she gets a better proposal from her point of view.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And the boys start going down their list, proposing to their first, second, third choices, until stopping when a proposal is accepted.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But the girls, meanwhile, are watching the proposals that are coming into them,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and the girl will drop her current partner if she gets a better proposal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And the boys never go back through the list?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: They never go back. Yeah. So once they've been denied...

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: They don't try again.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: They don't try again because the girls are always improving their status as they receive better and better proposals.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: The boys are going down their list, starting with their top preferences.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And one can prove that the process will come to an end, where everybody will get matched with somebody,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and you won't have any pair that want to abscond from each other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Do you find the proof or the algorithm itself beautiful?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Or is it the fact that with the simplicity of just the two marching...

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: I mean, the simplicity of the underlying rule of the algorithm, is that the beautiful part?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Both, I would say.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And you also have the observation that you might ask,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: who is better off, the boys who are doing the proposing or the girls who are reacting to proposals?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And it turns out that it's the boys who are doing the best.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And as each boy is doing at least as well as he could do in any other staple matching.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So there's a sort of lesson for the boys that you should go out and be proactive and make those proposals go for broke.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: I don't know if this is directly mappable philosophically to our society, but certainly seems like a compelling notion.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And like you said, there's probably a lot of actual real world problems that this could be mapped to.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: No, it's desirable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Desirable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Or at least go to the same city.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So you can't, if you're assigning residents to hospitals.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And then you have some preferences for the husband and wife or for the hospitals.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: The fact that you have this additional constraint, that it's not just the preferences of individuals,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: I'm being a little dense.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Okay, what's confusing you is that in the first interpretation of the problem, I had boys matching with girls.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Well, yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Okay. By the way, the algorithm you mentioned, was it one of yours?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: No, no, that was due to Gale and Shapley.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: My friend David Gale passed away before he could get part of a Nobel Prize,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So you've also developed yourself some elegant, beautiful algorithms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Again, picking your children. So the Robin Karp algorithm for string searching, pattern matching,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111
