metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Is there ones that stand out to you as ones you're most proud of or just

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: whether it's beauty, elegance, or just being the right discovery, development in your life that you're especially proud of?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: I like the Rabin Karp algorithm because it illustrates the power of randomization.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So the problem there is to decide whether a given long string of symbols from some alphabet contains a given word,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: whether a particular word occurs within some very much longer word.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And so the idea of the algorithm is to associate with the word that we're looking for a fingerprint,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: some number or some combinatorial object that describes that word,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and then to look for an occurrence of that same fingerprint as you slide along the longer word.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And what we do is we associate with each word a number.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So we first of all, we think of the letters that occur in a word as the digits of let's say decimal or whatever base here,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: whatever number of different symbols there are.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: That's the base of the numbers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Right. So every word can then be thought of as a number with the letters being the digits of that number.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And then we pick a random prime number in a certain range,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and we take that word viewed as a number and take the remainder on dividing that number by the prime.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So coming up with a nice hash function.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: It's a kind of hash function.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yeah. It gives you a little shortcut for that particular word.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yeah. So that's the...

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: It's very different than the other algorithms of its kind that we're trying to do search, string matching.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yeah, which usually are combinatorial and don't involve the idea of taking a random fingerprint.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And doing the fingerprinting has two advantages.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: One is that as we slide along the long word digit by digit, we keep a window of a certain size,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: the size of the word we're looking for, and we compute the fingerprint of every stretch of that length.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And it turns out that just a couple of arithmetical operations will take you from the fingerprint of one part

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: to what you get when you slide over by one position.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So the computation of all the fingerprints is simple.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And secondly, it's unlikely if the prime is chosen randomly from a certain range

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: that you will get two of the segments in question having the same fingerprint.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And so there's a small probability of error which can be checked after the fact,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and also the ease of doing the computation because you're working with these fingerprints,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: which are remainders, modulo, some big prime.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So that's the magical thing about randomized algorithms is that if you add a little bit of randomness,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: it somehow allows you to take a pretty naive approach, a simple looking approach,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and allow it to run extremely well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So can you maybe take a step back and say, like, what is a randomized algorithm, this category of algorithms?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Well, it's just the ability to draw a random number from such, from some range,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: or to associate a random number with some object, or to draw that random from some set.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So another example is very simple.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: If we're conducting a presidential election and we would like to pick the winner,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: in principle, we could draw a random sample of all of the voters in the country.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And if it was of substantial size, say a few thousand,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: then the most popular candidate in that group would be very likely to be the correct choice

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: that would come out of counting all the millions of votes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Now, of course, we can't do this because, first of all, everybody has to feel that his or her vote counted.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And secondly, we can't really do a purely random sample from that population.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And I guess thirdly, there could be a tie in which case we wouldn't have a significant difference between two candidates.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But those things aside, if you didn't have all that messiness of human beings,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: you could prove that that kind of random picking would come up.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: You guess that random picking would solve the problem with a very low probability of error.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Another example is testing whether a number is prime.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So if I want to test whether 17 is prime, I could pick any number between 1 and 17

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and raise it to the 16th power, modulo 17, and you should get back the original number.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: That's a famous formula due to Fermat.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: It's called Fermat's Little Theorem that if you take any number a in the range 0 through n minus 1

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and raise it to the n minus 1th power, modulo n, you'll get back the number a if a is prime.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So if you don't get back the number a, that's a proof that a number is not prime.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Oh.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And you can show that, suitably define the probability that you will get a value unequaled.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: You will get a violation of Fermat's result is very high,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and so this gives you a way of rapidly proving that a number is not prime.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: It's a little more complicated than that because there are certain values of n

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: where something a little more elaborate has to be done, but that's the basic idea.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Taking an identity that holds for primes and therefore if it ever fails on any instance for a non-prime unit,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: you know that the number is not prime.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: It's a quick choice, a fast choice, fast proof that a number is not prime.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Can you maybe elaborate a little bit more, what's your intuition why randomness works so well

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and results in such simple algorithms?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Well, the example of conducting an election where you could take, in theory you could take a sample

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and depend on the validity of the sample to really represent the whole is just the basic fact of statistics

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: which gives a lot of opportunities.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: I actually exploited that sort of random sampling idea in designing an algorithm for counting the number of solutions

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: that satisfy a particular formula and propositional logic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: A particular, so some version of the satisfiability problem?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Or a version of the satisfiability problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Is there some interesting insight that you want to elaborate on, like what some aspect of that algorithm

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: that might be useful to describe?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So you have a collection of formulas and you want to count the number of solutions that satisfy at least one of the formulas.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And you can count the number of solutions that satisfy any particular one of the formulas,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: but you have to account for the fact that that solution might be counted many times if it solves more than one of the formulas.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And so what you do is you sample from the formulas according to the number of solutions that satisfy each individual one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And that way you draw a random solution, but then you correct by looking at the number of formulas that satisfy that random solution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And don't double count.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So you can think of it this way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So you have a matrix of zeros and ones.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And you want to know how many columns of that matrix contain at least one one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And you can count in each row how many ones there are.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So what you can do is draw from the rows according to the number of ones. If a row has more ones, it gets drawn more frequently.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But then if you draw from that row, you have to go up the column and looking at where that same one is repeated in different rows.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And only count it as a success or a hit if it's the earliest row that contains the one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And that gives you a robust statistical estimate of the total number of columns that contain at least one of the ones.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So that is an example of the same principle that was used in studying random sampling.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Another viewpoint is that if you have a phenomenon that occurs almost all the time, then if you sample one of the occasions where it occurs,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: you're most likely to – and you're looking for an occurrence, a random occurrence is likely to work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So that comes up in solving identities, solving algebraic identities.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: You get two formulas that may look very different. You want to know if they're really identical.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: What you can do is just pick a random value and evaluate the formulas at that value and seeing if they agree.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And you depend on the fact that if the formulas are distinct, then they're going to disagree a lot.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And so therefore, a random choice will exhibit the disagreement.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: If there are many ways for the two to disagree and you only need to find one disagreement, then random choice is likely to yield it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And in general, so we've just talked about randomized algorithms, but we can look at the probabilistic analysis of algorithms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And that gives us an opportunity to step back. And as we said, everything we've been talking about is worst-case analysis.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Because you maybe comment on the usefulness and the power of worst-case analysis versus best-case analysis, average case, probabilistic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: How do we think about the future of theoretical computer science, computer science, and the kind of analysis we do of algorithms?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Does worst-case analysis still have a place, an important place, or do we want to try to move forward towards kind of average case analysis?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And what are the challenges there?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So if worst-case analysis shows that an algorithm is always good, that's fine.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: If worst-case analysis is used to show that the problem, that the solution is not always good, then you have to step back and do something else to ask, how often will you get a good solution?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Just to pause on that for a second, that's so beautifully put because I think we tend to judge algorithms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: We throw them in the trash the moment their worst case is shown to be bad.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Right. And that's unfortunate. I think a good example is going back to the satisfiability problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: There are very powerful programs called SAT solvers, which in practice fairly reliably solve instances with many millions of variables that arise in digital design or in proving programs correct in other applications.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And so in many application areas, even though satisfiability, as we've already discussed, is NP-complete, the SAT solvers will work so well that the people in that discipline tend to think of satisfiability as an easy problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So in other words, just for some reason that we don't entirely understand, the instances that people formulate in designing digital circuits or other applications are such that satisfiability is not hard to check.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And even searching for a satisfying solution can be done efficiently in practice.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And there are many examples. For example, we talked about the traveling salesman problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So just to refresh our memories, the problem is you've got a set of cities, you have pairwise distances between cities,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and you want to find a tour through all the cities that minimizes the total cost of all the edges traversed, all the trips between cities.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: The problem is NP-hard, but people using integer programming codes together with some other mathematical tricks can solve geometric instances of the problem where the cities are, let's say, points in the plane

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and get optimal solutions to problems with tens of thousands of cities. Actually, it'll take a few computer months to solve a problem of that size,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: but for problems of size 1,000 or 2, it'll rapidly get optimal solutions, provably optimal solutions,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: even though, again, we know that it's unlikely that the traveling salesman problem can be solved in polynomial time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Are there methodologies, like rigorous systematic methodologies for, you said in practice, in practice this algorithm sounds pretty good.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Are there systematic ways of saying in practice this one sounds pretty good? So in other words, average case analysis.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Or you've also mentioned that average case kind of requires you to understand what the typical case is, typical instances, and that might be really difficult.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: That's very difficult. So after I did my original work on getting, showing all these problems to be NP-complete,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: I looked around for a way to shed some positive light on combinatorial algorithms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And what I tried to do was to study problems, behavior on the average or with high probability.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But I had to make some assumptions about what's the probability space, what's the sample space, what do we mean by typical problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: That's very hard to say. So I took the easy way out and made some very simplistic assumptions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So I assumed, for example, that if we were generating a graph with a certain number of vertices and edges,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: then we would generate the graph by simply choosing one edge at a time at random until we got the right number of edges.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: That's a particular model of random graphs that has been studied mathematically a lot.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And within that model, I could prove all kinds of wonderful things, I and others who also worked on this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So we could show that we know exactly how many edges there have to be in order for there to be a so-called Hamiltonian circuit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: That's a cycle that visits each vertex exactly once.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: We know that if the number of edges is a little bit more than n log n, where n is the number of vertices,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: then such a cycle is very likely to exist. And we can give a heuristic that will find it with high probability.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And the community in which I was working got a lot of results along these lines.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But the field tended to be rather lukewarm about accepting these results as meaningful

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: because we were making such a simplistic assumption about the kinds of graphs that we would be dealing with.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So we could show all kinds of wonderful things. It was a great playground. I enjoyed doing it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But after a while, I concluded that it didn't have a lot of bite in terms of the practical application.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: OK, so there's too much into the world of toy problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: OK, but is there a way to find nice representative real world impactful instances of a problem on which demonstrate that an algorithm is good?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So this is kind of like the machine learning world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: That's kind of what they at its best tries to do is find a data set from the real world and show the performance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: All the conferences are all focused on beating the performance on that real world data set.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Is there an equivalent in complexity analysis?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Not really. Don Knuth started to collect examples of graphs coming from various places.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So he would have a whole zoo of different graphs that he could choose from and he could study the performance of algorithms on different types of graphs.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But there it's really important and compelling to be able to define a class of graphs.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: The actual act of defining a class of graphs that you're interested in seems to be a non-trivial step if we're talking about instances that we should care about in the real world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yeah, there's nothing available there that would be analogous to the training set for supervised learning,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: where you sort of assume that the world has given you a bunch of examples to work with.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: We don't really have that for problems, for combinatorial problems on graphs and networks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: There's been a huge growth, a big growth of data sets available.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Do you think some aspect of theoretical computer science, I might be contradicting my own question while saying it,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: but will there be some aspect, an empirical aspect of theoretical computer science which will allow the fact that these data sets are huge, will start using them for analysis?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: If you want to say something about a graph algorithm, you might take a social network like Facebook and looking at sub graphs of that and prove something about the Facebook graph

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and at the same time be respected in the theoretical computer science community.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: That hasn't been achieved yet, I'm afraid.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Is that P equals NP? Is that impossible?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Is it impossible to publish a successful paper in the theoretical computer science community that shows some performance on a real world data set?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Or is that really just those two different worlds?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: They haven't really come together. I would say that there is a field of experimental algorithmics where people, sometimes they're given some family of examples.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Sometimes they just generate them at random and they report on performance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But there's no convincing evidence that the sample is representative of anything at all.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Let me ask, in terms of breakthroughs and open problems, what are the most compelling open problems to you and what possible breakthroughs do you see in the near term in terms of theoretical computer science?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Well, there are all kinds of relationships among complexity classes that can be studied.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Just to mention one thing, I wrote a paper with Richard Lipton in 1979 where we asked the following question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: If you take a combinatorial problem in NP, let's say, and you pick the size of the problem, say it's a traveling salesman problem, but of size 52,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and you ask, could you get an efficient, a small Boolean circuit tailored for that size 52 where you could feed the edges of the graph in as Boolean inputs

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: and get as an output the question of whether or not there's a tour of a certain length.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And that would, in other words, briefly what you would say in that case is that the problem has small circuits, polynomial size circuits.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Now, we know that if P is equal to NP, then in fact these problems will have small circuits.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But what about the converse?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Could a problem have small circuits, meaning that it's, that an algorithm tailored to any particular size could work well?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And yet not be a polynomial time algorithm.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: That is, you couldn't write it as a single uniform algorithm good for all sizes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Just to clarify, small circuits for a problem of particular size or even further constraint, small circuit for a particular?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: No, for all the inputs of that size.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Of that size.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Is that a trivial problem for a particular instance?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So coming up, an automated way of coming up with a circuit, I guess that's just an-

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: That would be hard.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But there's the existential question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Everybody talks nowadays about existential questions, existential challenges.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: You could ask the question, does the Hamiltonian circuit problem have a small circuit for every size, for each size a different small circuit?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: In other words, could you tailor solutions depending on the size and get polynomial size?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Even if P is not equal to NP.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And-

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: That would be fascinating if that's true.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: What we proved is that if that were possible, then something strange would happen in complexity theory.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Some high level class, which I could briefly describe, something strange would happen.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So I'll take a stab at describing what I mean by this class.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Sure. Let's go there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So we have to define this hierarchy in which the first level of the hierarchy is P and the second level is NP.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And what is NP? NP involves statements of the form there exists a something such that something holds.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So for example, there exists a coloring such that a graph can be colored with only that number of colors or there exists a Hamiltonian circuit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: There's a statement about this graph.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So the NP deals with statements of that kind, that there exists a solution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Now you could imagine a more complicated expression which says for all X there exists a Y such that some proposition holds involving both X and Y.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So that would say, for example, in game theory, for all strategies for the first player there exists a strategy for the second player such that the first player wins.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: That would be at the second level of the hierarchy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: The third level would be there exists an A such that for all B there exists a C that something holds.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And you can imagine going higher and higher in the hierarchy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And you'd expect that the complexity classes that correspond to those different cases would get bigger and bigger.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: What do you mean by bigger and bigger?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Sorry. They'd get harder and harder to solve.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And what Lipton and I showed was that if NP had small circuits, then this hierarchy would collapse down to the second level.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: In other words, you wouldn't get any more mileage by complicating your expressions with three quantifiers or four quantifiers or any number.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: I'm not sure what to make of that exactly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Well, I think it would be evidence that NP doesn't have small circuits because something so bizarre would happen.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But again, it's only evidence, not proof.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Well, yeah, that's not even evidence because you're saying P is not equal to NP because something bizarre has to happen.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: I mean, that's proof by the lack of bizarreness in our science.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But it seems like just the very notion of P equals NP would be bizarre.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So any way you arrive at it, there's no way. You have to fight the dragon at some point.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yeah. Okay. Well, anyway, for whatever it's worth, that's what we proved.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Awesome. So that's a potential space of open interesting problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Let me ask you about this other world of machine learning, of deep learning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: What's your thoughts on the history and the current progress of machine learning field that's often progressed sort of separately as a space of ideas and space of people than the theoretical computer science or just even computer science world?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yeah. It's really very different from the theoretical computer science world because the results about it, algorithmic performance, tend to be empirical.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: It's more akin to the world of SAT solvers where we observe that for formulas arising in practice, the solver does well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So it's of that type. We're moving into the empirical evaluation of algorithms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Now, it's clear that there have been huge successes in image processing, robotics, natural language processing, a little less so.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But across the spectrum of game playing is another one. There have been great successes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And one of those effects is that it's not too hard to become a millionaire if you can get a reputation in machine learning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: There'll be all kinds of companies that will be willing to offer you the moon because they think that if they have AI at their disposal, then they can solve all kinds of problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But there are limitations. One is that the solutions that you get to supervise learning problems through convolutional neural networks

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: seem to perform amazingly well, even for inputs that are outside the training set.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But we don't have any theoretical understanding of why that's true.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Secondly, the solutions, the networks that you get are very hard to understand, and so very little insight comes out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So yeah, yeah, they may seem to work on your training set, and you may be able to discover whether your photos occur in a different sample of inputs or not.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But we don't really know what's going on. We don't know the features that distinguish the photographs or the objects are not easy to characterize.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Well, it's interesting because you mentioned coming up with a small circuit to solve a particular size problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: It seems that neural networks are kind of small circuits.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: In a way, yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But they're not programs. Sort of like the things you've designed are algorithms, programs, algorithms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Neural networks aren't able to develop algorithms to solve a problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Well, they are.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: They are algorithms. It's just that they're...

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But sort of, yeah, it could be a semantic question, but there's not an algorithmic style manipulation of the input.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Perhaps you could argue there is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yeah, well...

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: It feels a lot more like a function of the input.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yeah, it's a function. It's a computable function.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Once you have the network, you can simulate it on a given input and figure out the output.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But if you're trying to recognize images, then you don't know what features of the image are really being determinant of what the circuit is doing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: The circuit is sort of very intricate, and it's not clear that the simple characteristics that you're looking for, the edges of the objects or whatever they may be, they're not emerging from the structure of the circuit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Well, it's not clear to us humans, but it's clear to the circuit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yeah. Well, right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: I mean, it's not clear to sort of the elephant how the human brain works, but it's clear to us humans we can explain to each other our reasoning, and that's why the cognitive science and psychology field exists.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Maybe the whole thing of being explainable to humans is a little bit overrated.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Oh, maybe. Yeah. I guess you can say the same thing about our brain that when we perform acts of cognition, we have no idea how we do it, really.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: We do, though. I mean, at least for the visual system, the auditory system, and so on, we do get some understanding of the principles that they operate under, but for many deeper cognitive tasks, we don't have that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: That's right. Let me ask. Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: You've also been doing work on bioinformatics. Does it amaze you that the fundamental building blocks, if we take a step back and look at us humans, the building blocks used by evolution to build us intelligent human beings is all contained there in our DNA.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: It's amazing, and what's really amazing is that we are beginning to learn how to edit DNA, which is very, very, very fascinating, this ability to take a sequence,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: find it in the genome and do something to it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: I mean, that's really taking our biological system towards the world of algorithms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yeah, but it raises a lot of questions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: You have to distinguish between doing it on an individual or doing it on somebody's germline, which means that all of the descendants will be affected.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So that's like an ethical...

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yeah, so it raises very severe ethical questions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: And even doing it on individuals, there's a lot of hubris involved that you can assume that knocking out a particular gene is going to be beneficial because you don't know what the side effects are going to be.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So we have this wonderful new world of gene editing, which is very, very impressive, and it could be used in agriculture.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: It could be used in medicine in various ways, but very serious ethical problems arise.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: What are to you the most interesting places where algorithms...

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Sort of the ethical side is an exceptionally challenging thing that I think we're going to have to tackle with all of genetic engineering.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: But on the algorithmic side, there's a lot of benefit that's possible.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So is there areas where you see exciting possibilities for algorithms to help model, optimize, study biological systems?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Yeah, I mean, we can certainly analyze genomic data to figure out which genes are operative in the cell and under what conditions and which proteins affect one another, which proteins physically interact.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: We can sequence proteins and modify them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Is there some aspect of that that's a computer science problem or is that still fundamentally a biology problem?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Well, it's a big data. It's a statistical big data problem for sure.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: So the biological data sets are increasing, our ability to study our ancestry, to study the tendencies towards disease, to personalize treatment according to what's in our genomes and what tendencies for disease we have,

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: to be able to predict what troubles might come upon us in the future and anticipate them to understand whether you...

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: For a woman, whether her proclivity for breast cancer is strong enough that you would want to take action to avoid it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: You dedicate your 1985 Turing Award lecture to the memory of your father.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: What's your fondest memory of your dad?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Seeing him standing in front of a class at the blackboard, drawing perfect circles by hand and showing his ability to attract the interest of the motley collection of eighth grade students that he was teaching.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: When did you get a chance to see him draw the perfect circles?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: On rare occasions, I would get a chance to sneak into his classroom and observe him.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: I think he was at his best in the classroom. I think he really came to life and had fun not only teaching, but engaging in chit chat with the students and ingratiating himself with the students.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: What I inherited from that is the great desire to be a teacher. I retired recently and a lot of my former students came, students with whom I had done research or who had read my papers or who had been in my classes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: When they talked about me, they talked not about my 1979 paper or my 1992 paper, but about what came away in my classes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Not just the details, but just the approach and the manner of teaching. I take pride in the, at least in my early years as a faculty member at Berkeley, I was exemplary in preparing my lectures.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: I always came in prepared to the teeth and able therefore to deviate according to what happened in the class and to really provide a model for the students.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Is there advice you can give out for others on how to be a good teacher? Preparation is one thing you've mentioned, being exceptionally well prepared. Are there other pieces of advice that you can impart?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: The top three would be preparation, preparation, and preparation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: Why is preparation so important, I guess?

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

body.input: It's because it gives you the ease to deal with any situation that comes up in the classroom. If you discover that you're not getting through one way, you can do it another way. If the students have questions, you can handle the questions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Richard Karp: Algorithms and Computational Complexity | Lex Fridman Podcast #111

metadata.title: Podcast: Ann Druyan: Cosmos, Carl Sagan, Voyager, and the Beauty of Science | Lex Fridman Podcast #78

body.input: Thank you.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ann Druyan: Cosmos, Carl Sagan, Voyager, and the Beauty of Science | Lex Fridman Podcast #78

body.input: All right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ann Druyan: Cosmos, Carl Sagan, Voyager, and the Beauty of Science | Lex Fridman Podcast #78

body.input: Let's move on to another book.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ann Druyan: Cosmos, Carl Sagan, Voyager, and the Beauty of Science | Lex Fridman Podcast #78

body.input: This one is called FLEX FREEDMAN.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ann Druyan: Cosmos, Carl Sagan, Voyager, and the Beauty of Science | Lex Fridman Podcast #78

body.input: And now, let me leave you some words of wisdom from Carl Sagan.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ann Druyan: Cosmos, Carl Sagan, Voyager, and the Beauty of Science | Lex Fridman Podcast #78

body.input: What an astonishing thing a book is. It's a flat object made from a tree with flexible parts

metadata.title: Podcast: Ann Druyan: Cosmos, Carl Sagan, Voyager, and the Beauty of Science | Lex Fridman Podcast #78

body.input: on which are imprinted lots of funny dark squiggles. But one glance at it,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ann Druyan: Cosmos, Carl Sagan, Voyager, and the Beauty of Science | Lex Fridman Podcast #78

body.input: and you're inside the mind of another person, maybe somebody dead for thousands of years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ann Druyan: Cosmos, Carl Sagan, Voyager, and the Beauty of Science | Lex Fridman Podcast #78

body.input: your head directly to you. Writing is perhaps the greatest of human inventions, binding together

metadata.title: Podcast: Ann Druyan: Cosmos, Carl Sagan, Voyager, and the Beauty of Science | Lex Fridman Podcast #78

body.input: people who never knew each other, citizens of distant epochs. Books break the shackles of time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ann Druyan: Cosmos, Carl Sagan, Voyager, and the Beauty of Science | Lex Fridman Podcast #78

body.input: A book is proof that humans are capable of working magic. Thank you for listening and hope to see you
